summary: Most YANG modules model devices or monolithic functions, but some model network services, such as the L3 VPN service model. This informational document explains what service models are, how they are used and how they relate to device configuration models.

plainLanguage.summary: A customer service model describes what a customer requests or receives from a network operator. Separate models describe how the operator maps that request to network services, controllers, and devices.

subtitle: How customer-facing service models differ from models used to configure a provider's network.

tldr.problem: Customers need a way to describe requested network services without specifying how a provider engineers its network to deliver them.
tldr.mechanism: A customer service model formally describes the service at the customer-provider interface, while separate service-delivery and device models describe provider implementation.
tldr.outcome: The RFC clarifies the terms and their possible place in an SDN architecture. It does not assume a particular delivery technology or define a protocol for exchanging models.

today: RFC 8309 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: What a Customer Service Model Describes
sections.content:
The memo describes service models in the IETF's YANG work. A service model is a formal representation of data elements that describe a network service as a customer requests or experiences it. The service could be Internet connectivity, a virtual circuit, or a multi-site virtual private network.

A customer service model is distinct from the way a provider realizes the service inside its network. It can be technology agnostic so the customer describes the desired service without specifying the provider's internal protocols, devices, or topology. Technology details are included when they directly affect the customer-facing service.
sections.plainLanguage: A customer service model describes the service from the customer's point of view. It does not normally describe the provider's internal equipment or path choices.

sections.title: Customer Models and Delivery Models
sections.content:
The memo distinguishes a customer service model from a service delivery model. A customer model describes what the provider offers or delivers to a customer and can be used to request or configure a service. A service delivery model is used by the provider to manage how the service is engineered in its network.

Customer service models are not sent directly to routers or switches for processing. The provider maps the customer's request into operational parameters and may use service-delivery models to instruct network orchestrators or controllers. Network-element models describe still lower-level configuration for individual devices.
sections.plainLanguage: The customer-facing model says what service is wanted. Provider-side models translate that request into network and device configuration.

sections.title: Service Models in an SDN Architecture
sections.content:
In a possible SDN arrangement, a customer provides a service model to a service orchestrator. The orchestrator maps the request to provider policies and technology choices, then may create service delivery models for network orchestrators. Controllers and network-element models are used farther down the chain to configure devices.

The customer-facing service request should generally remain independent of the technology used to fulfill it. The RFC notes that the internal organization of an SDN control plane depends on deployment, and that service models neither require nor preclude SDN.
sections.plainLanguage: A service orchestrator can translate a customer's service request into instructions for provider systems. The customer need not select the technologies used inside the provider's network.

sections.title: Scope, Extensions, and Similar Terms
sections.content:
The memo warns against confusing network connectivity services with value-added services such as storage or software services. It also distinguishes a service model from the actual service and from a Service Level Agreement. Commercial terms and detailed SLA rules vary among providers and are not generally suitable for a common base model.

A standardized customer service model can define a shared core and allow operator-specific extensions or augmentations. Separate models may be used for separate services. Policy features should be easy to add, while the base model should focus on customer-influenced service parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: A model describes a service; it is not the service itself or the full commercial agreement. A common model can provide shared fields while allowing providers to add their own options.

sections.title: Security and Manageability
sections.content:
The customer-provider interface needs appropriate confidentiality, authorization, authentication, and encryption. Modified or forged service requests can cause incorrect expectations, unwarranted billing, or traffic delivery to the wrong place. Other external interfaces between functional components also need protection.

Automated provisioning can change traffic loads quickly and affect other services. The memo expects service orchestration to account for existing commitments and network orchestration to avoid committing resources when it is not appropriate. Feedback should report degradation that affects a service.
sections.plainLanguage: Service requests must be protected from unauthorized changes. Automated provisioning also needs to account for other services that share the same network resources.
